This modest initial size belies the substantial growth trajectory the cub must undergo before achieving nutritional independence. Maternal investment during the early postpartum period is intensive, with the cub remaining fully dependent on the female for warmth and milk. This accelerated weaning schedule is an adaptation to the seasonal fruit pulses of the Andean cloud forest, allowing the female to terminate lactation and resume foraging for high-energy bromeliads and fruits.

Reproduction in the spectacled bear proceeds at a characteristically slow pace for a mammal of its size. This prolonged gestation is followed by a significant period of maternal care that delays the development of reproductive functionality in the offspring. This protracted juvenile phase is critical for learning complex foraging techniques, such as extracting palm nuts and climbing to access epiphytic bromeliads. The delay also reflects the time required to accrue sufficient body mass to compete for territories and mates, as a young bear attempting to breed earlier would likely face severe energetic constraints.

The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in body size, a trait that has direct implications for life history scheduling. Adult males in prime condition regularly achieve an ultimate wet weight of 115 kilograms [Wwi = 115 kilograms], with exceptional individuals in the upper Andean foothills documented near the 200-kilogram mark. This disparity is among the most extreme within the Ursidae, rivaling that of the brown bear. The reproductive output of the species is correspondingly low, constrained by the high costs of gestation and prolonged lactation under a low-quality, largely frugivorous diet. This two-pup litter is the standard, though single cubs are not uncommon.
